strengths: The paper addresses an important problem for visual robot simulation: compounding errors when action-conditioned video models consume their own predictions. The shared-prefix branching protocol is clearly motivated and compatible with existing diffusion backbones.

Table 1 shows consistent improvements over the reproduced Ctrl-World baseline across all views and metrics, including external-camera PSNR increasing from 23.02 to 24.42 and wrist-camera LPIPS decreasing from 0.310 to 0.277. The qualitative examples support improved object and robot persistence.

Evaluation goes beyond full-frame reconstruction. Object- and robot-masked results support improvements in relevant foreground regions, and the blinded, position-randomized human study reports 174 preferences against 43 for the baseline.
Appendix C provides useful preliminary downstream evidence: across three tasks and three policies, policy-performance correlation improves from 0.796 to 0.822 and MMRV decreases from 0.053 to 0.006.

The manuscript appropriately attributes DiffusionNFT and acknowledges the closely related WorldCompass training paradigm. It supplies extensive ablations, pseudocode, compute requirements, and a reasonable discussion of the limitations of visual rewards.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the central benefit of contrastive RL from additional training and exposure to generated histories. Important controls include compute-matched supervised fine-tuning, supervised training with self-generated contexts, and reward-weighted or positive-only updates. Without these, the gains over the pretrained backbone do not establish which proposed mechanism is necessary.

The claimed convergence and policy-improvement guarantees exceed Appendix A's result. Theorem 1 identifies an idealized pointwise denoising-loss minimizer; it does not establish convergence of the training algorithm or increased expected reward of sampled autoregressive trajectories. Its derivation assumes samples from the reference distribution and an exact reference posterior-mean predictor, whereas Algorithm 1 samples from the current model and updates an EMA reference. Group-dependent normalization and extreme-candidate filtering further require justification. Also, the statement that beta approaching zero recovers supervised denoising is incorrect: at beta equal to zero, the loss is independent of the trainable predictor.

The empirical support for randomized prefix depth, a principal distinction from related work, is weak. Contrary to the text accompanying Table 5, random 0–9 does not match or exceed every fixed baseline: fixed size 3 has better wrist results on all three metrics. Against the curriculum, random 0–9 improves three metrics, ties two, and worsens wrist PSNR. These small differences lack uncertainty estimates and do not establish the claimed advantage.

Several implementation and evaluation details hinder reproducibility. Appendix A describes a reference frozen throughout training, while Algorithm 1 and Table 10 update it. The default KL regularizer lacks a specified formula and coefficient; beta and the training noise distribution are unspecified. The RL training split and its separation from evaluation need explicit identification, particularly because reward targets are repeatedly called held-out ground truth. The reported 70 frames at 5 Hz also do not correspond to approximately 11 seconds.

Evidence for reliable simulation remains preliminary. The primary metrics are also the optimized rewards, and masked image similarity does not directly establish accurate contact dynamics or action following. Appendix C is valuable but uses only five real rollouts per task-policy pair; both models overestimate task progression, and no uncertainty is given for their performance difference. The human study also permits participants to select videos, and its significance analysis does not explain how repeated raters and shared clips are handled.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem for robot video world models: compounding errors when generated frames become subsequent conditioning inputs. Training on self-generated histories is well motivated, and the shared-prefix branching procedure is clearly explained.

The empirical improvements over the reproduced Ctrl-World baseline are substantial and consistent across camera views. Table 1 reports external-camera PSNR improving from 23.02 to 24.42 dB and wrist-camera LPIPS decreasing from 0.310 to 0.277. The qualitative examples support improved object and robot persistence.

The evaluation goes beyond full-frame metrics. Object- and robot-masked measurements improve across all reported metrics, and the blinded, position-randomized human study favors the proposed model in 174 of 217 judgments. These provide useful complementary evidence of perceptually meaningful improvements.

The appendix includes extensive hyperparameter ablations and an initial downstream policy-evaluation experiment. The manuscript appropriately attributes its backbone and contrastive objective and acknowledges that visual rewards do not explicitly enforce physical consistency.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, the distinct methodological contribution is insufficiently established. The paper acknowledges that contemporary WorldCompass already combines contrastive diffusion post-training with self-generated prefixes. The principal distinctions here are the affine x0 adaptation, randomized prefix lengths, and multi-view metric rewards. Yet Table 5 does not establish an advantage for randomized prefixes: fixed size 3 is better on all three wrist metrics and external PSNR. The text's claim that the proposed strategy matches or exceeds every fixed baseline is therefore unsupported.

The experiments do not isolate the source of the gains. Comparisons against the original checkpoint cannot distinguish the proposed RL objective from additional adaptation or exposure to generated histories. Important controls include continued supervised fine-tuning, supervised denoising conditioned on generated or perturbed histories, and the same contrastive objective with no generated prefix. Without these, the necessity and incremental benefit of the proposed training mechanism remain unclear.

The theoretical claims exceed the result proved. Appendix A establishes a pointwise minimizer of a surrogate denoising loss under idealized assumptions; it does not establish convergence of the iterative training procedure or monotonic improvement of generated-rollout rewards. The proof assumes reference-distributed samples and an exact reference posterior-mean denoiser, whereas Algorithm 1 samples from the current model and uses an EMA reference, group-dependent rewards, and sample filtering. These differences are not covered. Moreover, the statement that beta approaching zero recovers supervised denoising is incorrect for Eq. 2: at beta zero, both branches equal the frozen reference and the loss has no gradient with respect to the current model.

Reproducibility and evaluation protocols need clarification. The post-training dataset subset and its separation from evaluation are not explicitly specified, despite repeated references to reward computation against 'held-out' ground truth. The beta value, noise-level sampling distribution, and KL regularization formula and coefficient are missing. Appendix A describes a reference that is never updated, conflicting with the EMA implementation. There are also unexplained protocol inconsistencies: 70 frames at 5 Hz do not correspond to approximately 11 seconds, and the temporal plots extend only to about 50 frames.

The evidence supports improved visual reconstruction more strongly than reliable interaction simulation. The primary evaluation metrics are also the training rewards, and masked image similarity alone does not establish correct contact dynamics or action following. Appendix C is a useful initial check, but it contains only three tasks and three policies, with five real trials per task-policy pair. The correlation increase from 0.796 to 0.822 lacks uncertainty on the difference, while both models overestimate task progress. Strong claims about reliable simulators therefore remain premature.

Several statistical and ablation interpretations require correction. The human study uses eight in-house participants who can select which videos to rate; repeated judgments and video selection complicate the independent-binomial significance claim, and the reported 95% interval of [72%, 100%] is unexplained. Most ablation differences are small and have no seed variability or uncertainty estimates. Table 6 also shows that both no filtering and best-of-2 outperform the chosen best-of-5 configuration on every metric, without evidence substantiating the claimed stability tradeoff.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem for visual robot simulation: compounding errors when action-conditioned video models consume their own predictions. The shared-prefix branching protocol provides a practical way to apply contrastive diffusion post-training to this setting.

The improvements over the reproduced Ctrl-World baseline are substantial and consistent. Table 1 reports external-camera PSNR increasing from 23.02 to 24.42 and wrist-camera PSNR from 17.80 to 19.39, with corresponding improvements in SSIM and LPIPS.

The evaluation extends beyond full-frame reconstruction. Object- and robot-masked results improve across all reported metrics, and the blinded human study favors the proposed model in 174 of 217 comparisons. These provide complementary evidence that the gains are perceptually meaningful.

Appendix C includes a useful preliminary connection to downstream policy evaluation: real-to-sim task-progress correlation increases from 0.796 to 0.822, while MMRV decreases from 0.053 to 0.006. The paper also appropriately acknowledges computational overhead and the absence of explicit physical constraints.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, the central contribution is insufficiently isolated. The paper acknowledges that WorldCompass already combines contrastive diffusion RL with generated prefixes. Comparisons against additional supervised fine-tuning, supervised training on generated histories, and RL without generated prefixes are missing. Consequently, the experiments do not establish how much improvement specifically requires the proposed RL treatment of exposure bias.

The claimed advantage of randomized prefix lengths is not supported by Table 5 as described. Fixed size 3 is better on four of six metrics, and the curriculum is better on wrist PSNR; randomized 0–9 prefixes outperform the curriculum on four metrics, with one tie, rather than five. Differences are small and lack uncertainty estimates. This matters because prefix randomization is a principal distinction from the closest related method.

Appendix A identifies an idealized pointwise denoising-loss minimizer; it does not prove convergence of the implemented training loop or improved expected reward after sampling. The proof assumes samples from the reference distribution and an exact reference posterior-mean predictor, whereas Algorithm 1 samples from the current model and updates an EMA reference. Group-dependent rewards and top/bottom selection also require reconciliation with the analysis. Additionally, the statement that beta approaching zero recovers supervised denoising is incorrect for Eq. 2: at beta zero, the loss is independent of the trainable predictor.

Important reproducibility details remain unclear. Reward computation repeatedly uses the phrase 'held-out ground truth,' but the post-training data partition and its separation from evaluation are not explicitly specified. This is an ambiguity, not evidence of leakage. Evaluation sample counts, the numerical beta setting, and the KL term and coefficient used in the default configuration are also missing.

Evidence for reliable simulation remains preliminary. Training directly optimizes the three main evaluation metrics, and masked image similarity alone does not establish correct interaction dynamics. The policy experiment uses only three tasks, three policies, and five real trials per task-policy pair, without uncertainty on the improvement over baseline. The human study is supportive, but self-selected videos and repeated votes from eight raters require dependence-aware statistical analysis; the reported confidence interval is not adequately explained.
Overall, the empirical gains make this a close decision, but the missing causal comparisons and unsupported theoretical guarantees leave a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem for visual robot simulation: error accumulation when action-conditioned video models consume their own predictions. Training on generated histories is well motivated, and the shared-prefix branching protocol is clearly described.

The improvements over the reproduced Ctrl-World baseline are substantial and consistent across the main visual metrics. Table 1 reports external-camera LPIPS improving from 0.081 to 0.070 and wrist-camera PSNR from 17.80 to 19.39 dB. Object- and robot-masked evaluations provide useful evidence that improvements extend to foreground regions.

The evaluation includes complementary evidence beyond the optimized full-frame metrics: qualitative comparisons, an 80% human preference rate, experiments on Bridge and RT-1, and real-robot policy evaluation and improvement. These broaden the practical case for the method.

The implementation avoids differentiating through sampling and updates only LoRA adapters and the action encoder. The paper provides training costs, extensive hyperparameter ablations, and pseudocode, and appropriately acknowledges related work and limitations of purely visual rewards.
weaknesses: The claimed convergence and policy-improvement guarantees exceed what Appendix A establishes. Theorem 1 characterizes an idealized denoising-loss minimizer under samples from the reference distribution and an exact reference posterior mean; it does not establish convergence of the implemented optimization or improved expected reward after autoregressive sampling. Algorithm 1 instead samples from the current model, updates the reference by EMA, and the implementation additionally filters candidates and uses KL regularization. These differences are not covered by the proof. Also, the statement that beta approaching zero recovers supervised training is incorrect for Eq. (2): the loss becomes independent of the trainable predictor.

The distinct algorithmic contribution is insufficiently supported relative to DiffusionNFT and the acknowledged concurrent WorldCompass paradigm. The affine parameterization adaptation is straightforward, and Table 5 contradicts the claim that random prefixes match or exceed every fixed-prefix baseline: fixed size 3 is better on all three wrist metrics and external PSNR. Differences against the curriculum are very small and lack uncertainty estimates. The evidence supports a useful adaptation more strongly than the claimed superiority of the proposed protocol.

The closest supervised control substantially narrows the demonstrated benefit of the RL objective. Training on generated histories with ground-truth regression gives wrist SSIM/PSNR of 0.710/20.17 versus 0.721/20.40, with effectively identical reported LPIPS. No repeated-run uncertainty is supplied. Figure 13 compares gradient steps rather than total computation, so its approximately 10-fold convergence claim does not establish comparable wall-clock or sampling efficiency.

Important reproducibility and evaluation details remain unresolved. The manuscript does not clearly specify the post-training dataset partition, despite repeatedly calling reward targets held-out ground truth. The mixing coefficient, noise sampling distribution, and KL formulation and coefficient are not specified. Appendix A describes a permanently frozen reference, whereas Algorithm 1 and Table 10 update it. The 10-step ablation LPIPS values differ markedly from the 14-step main results without explaining the evaluation configuration, and 70 frames at 5 Hz do not correspond to the stated 11 seconds.

The human study supports a preference trend, but its statistical claims require more care. Eight in-house raters could select which videos to assess, and repeated ratings may be dependent. The binomial significance calculation does not address clustering by video or participant, and the reported 95% interval of [72%, 100%] is not explained. Unique-video counts and participant- or video-aware uncertainty would make this evidence more convincing.

The downstream robot results are encouraging but preliminary: policy correlation uses only nine task-policy combinations with five real trials each, and policy improvement uses five trials per block. The increase in correlation from 0.796 to 0.822 has no uncertainty assessment; significance of each correlation separately does not establish a significant improvement. Overall, the empirical merits make this a close decision, but the unsupported central guarantees and incomplete isolation of the methodological gains slightly favor rejection under Algorithms/General.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: accumulated visual errors in action-conditioned robot video rollouts. Training on generated histories is well motivated, and the proposed branching protocol is clearly described. I assess the submission as Algorithms/General.

The visual improvements over the reproduced Ctrl-World baseline are substantial and consistent. Table 1 reports external-camera PSNR improving from 23.02 to 24.42 and wrist-camera LPIPS decreasing from 0.310 to 0.277. Object- and robot-masked evaluations provide additional evidence that improvements extend beyond static backgrounds.

The evaluation has useful breadth: Bridge and RT-1 experiments demonstrate applicability beyond DROID, and the human study reports 174 preferences for the proposed model versus 43 for the baseline. These support practical value beyond optimizing full-frame numerical metrics.

The real-robot experiments strengthen the submission: policy-ranking MMRV improves from 0.053 to 0.006, and policy fine-tuning using generated rollouts improves average task progression from 0.558 to 0.667 relative to Ctrl-World data. The paper also appropriately acknowledges computational overhead and the absence of explicit physical constraints.
weaknesses: The claimed convergence and policy-improvement guarantees exceed what Appendix A establishes. Theorem 1 characterizes a pointwise denoising-loss minimizer under idealized assumptions; it does not establish convergence of iterative post-training or improvement in sampled long-horizon rollout reward. Its derivation assumes samples from the reference distribution and an exact reference posterior-mean predictor, whereas Algorithm 1 samples from the current model and updates an EMA reference. Group-dependent rewards and top/bottom filtering introduce further differences that are not covered. The affine branch construction is reasonable, but an exact transfer of guarantees to the implemented algorithm is not demonstrated.

The distinctive algorithmic contribution is modest relative to the acknowledged DiffusionNFT and contemporary WorldCompass paradigms, and the evidence for randomized prefixes is particularly weak. Contrary to Appendix B's claim that random sampling matches or exceeds every fixed-window baseline, Table 5 shows fixed size 3 outperforming the proposed default on all three wrist metrics and external PSNR. Differences from the curriculum are small and lack uncertainty estimates. This does not invalidate the practical adaptation, but weakens a central claimed advantage.

The comparison with training on generated histories leaves the incremental benefit of the contrastive objective uncertain. Against the self-forcing-style baseline, external PSNR improves only from 25.35 to 25.52, wrist PSNR from 20.17 to 20.40, and wrist LPIPS is unchanged at the reported precision. Multiple seeds and matched computational budgets are needed to assess these margins. Figure 13's approximately 10× claim compares training steps rather than wall-clock cost despite the proposed method's additional candidate generation.

Important implementation details are missing or inconsistent. The numerical mixing coefficient beta and the KL penalty's definition and weight are not specified. Appendix A describes a permanently frozen reference, while the method and algorithm use EMA updates. Algorithm 1 omits the reported top/bottom sample filtering and KL term. The statement that beta approaching zero recovers supervised denoising is also incorrect for Eq. 2 as written: with a frozen reference, its gradient with respect to the current model vanishes.

The evaluation protocol needs clarification before the broad state-of-the-art claim is fully convincing. Table 1 mixes reproduced results with numbers imported from prior work, without establishing identical rollout and metric protocols. The manuscript describes 70 frames at 5 Hz as approximately 11 seconds, while the temporal plots extend to 50 frames. It also repeatedly calls reward targets 'held-out' ground truth without clearly specifying the post-training data split and its separation from evaluation. These ambiguities require clarification, rather than constituting evidence of leakage.

The independent validation is encouraging but statistically limited. Eight in-house raters could choose which videos to evaluate, creating selection and repeated-rating dependencies that the reported binomial analysis does not address; the stated confidence interval also lacks an explained construction. Policy evaluation uses only five real trials per task-policy pair, and policy improvement uses five trials per block. Without uncertainty estimates, these experiments support feasibility more strongly than reliable simulator superiority. Overall, the empirical merits make this a close decision, but the theoretical overclaims and insufficiently established incremental advantages favor borderline rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem for visual robot simulation: compounding errors when action-conditioned video models consume their own predictions. The shared-prefix branching protocol provides a practical way to apply contrastive diffusion post-training to this setting.

The empirical improvements over the reproduced Ctrl-World baseline are consistent and meaningful. Table 1 reports external-camera PSNR increasing from 23.02 to 24.42 and LPIPS decreasing from 0.081 to 0.070, alongside improvements across all wrist-camera metrics. Object- and robot-masked evaluations provide additional evidence that gains extend to task-relevant regions.

The evaluation goes beyond the training reward metrics. Human raters prefer the proposed model in 174 of 217 comparisons, and experiments on Bridge and RT-1 demonstrate benefits across additional embodiments after dataset-specific training. The policy-evaluation and real-robot policy-improvement experiments provide encouraging evidence of practical utility.

The manuscript appropriately acknowledges DiffusionNFT and the closely related WorldCompass paradigm, includes a supervised baseline trained on generated histories, and reports extensive ablations. It also explicitly recognizes that visual rewards do not enforce physical or geometric consistency. Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, the empirical contribution supports a slight preference for acceptance.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims exceed what Appendix A establishes. Theorem 1 characterizes an idealized pointwise denoising-loss minimizer; it does not establish convergence of the implemented training procedure or monotonic improvement in sampled rollout reward. The proof assumes reference-distribution samples and an exact reference posterior mean, whereas Algorithm 1 samples from the current model and updates an EMA reference. Group-dependent rewards and extreme-sample filtering further require justification. Claims that convergence and policy-improvement guarantees carry over exactly should therefore be narrowed or supported by additional analysis.

The algorithmic novelty is incremental relative to DiffusionNFT and WorldCompass, making evidence for the distinguishing choices particularly important. Table 5 does not support the statement that randomized prefixes match or exceed every fixed-prefix baseline: fixed size 3 achieves better wrist metrics. Differences from the curriculum are also small and lack uncertainty estimates. The x0 adaptation and robotics-specific validation are useful, but the manuscript overstates the demonstrated advantage of its prefix strategy.

The improvement attributable specifically to the RL objective is less compelling than the improvement over the pretrained model. Against supervised regression on generated histories, external PSNR improves only from 25.35 to 25.52, while wrist LPIPS is unchanged at the reported precision. Repeated runs and matched computational budgets would help establish this advantage. Figure 13 measures training steps, so it does not establish a tenfold wall-clock efficiency improvement given the cost of sampling multiple candidates.

Reproducibility and evaluation protocols need clarification. The numerical mixing coefficient beta and the KL penalty's definition and weight are not specified. Appendix A describes a permanently frozen reference, while the implementation uses EMA updates. Ground-truth reward targets are repeatedly described as held-out, without clearly identifying the post-training split and its separation from evaluation. The reported 70 frames at 5 Hz also do not match the stated approximately 11-second duration. Imported baseline results require clearer confirmation of matching evaluation conditions.

The independent validation is promising but statistically limited. Eight in-house raters could select which videos to judge, and repeated ratings introduce dependence that a simple binomial test does not address; the reported confidence interval also needs explanation. Policy evaluation uses only five real trials per task-policy pair, and policy improvement uses five trials per block. These results support feasibility, but do not yet firmly establish the reliability of the simulator for policy ranking or improvement.
